solution:
For a cell of emf \(\varepsilon\) and internal resistance \(r\) driving an external resistance \(R\), the current is \(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r}\). This is largest when \(R\) is smallest, i.e. when the terminals are short-circuited (\(R = 0\)), so the internal resistance alone limits the current.
Hence
\(I_{\max} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{r} = \dfrac{12\,\text{V}}{0.4\,\Omega}\)
Maximum current \(= 30\,\text{A}\).

The cell drives the current through the external resistor \(R\) in series with its own internal resistance \(r\), so \(\varepsilon = I(R + r)\).
\(R + r = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{I} = \dfrac{10\,\text{V}}{0.5\,\text{A}} = 20\,\Omega\)
\(R = 20\,\Omega - 3\,\Omega = 17\,\Omega\)
The terminal voltage is the emf less the drop across the internal resistance:
\(V = \varepsilon - Ir = 10\,\text{V} - (0.5\,\text{A})(3\,\Omega) = 8.5\,\text{V}\)
(Equivalently \(V = IR = (0.5\,\text{A})(17\,\Omega) = 8.5\,\text{V}\).)
Resistance of the resistor \(= 17\,\Omega\); terminal voltage \(= 8.5\,\text{V}\).

Take the resistance to vary with temperature as \(R_2 = R_1\left[1 + \alpha (T_2 - T_1)\right]\), with \(R_1 = 100\,\Omega\) at \(T_1 = 27.0\,^\circ\text{C}\) and \(R_2 = 117\,\Omega\).
\(T_2 - T_1 = \dfrac{R_2 - R_1}{R_1\,\alpha} = \dfrac{117\,\Omega - 100\,\Omega}{(100\,\Omega)\left(1.70 \times 10^{-4}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\right)}\)
\(T_2 - T_1 = \dfrac{17}{1.70 \times 10^{-2}} = 1000\,^\circ\text{C}\)
\(T_2 = 1000\,^\circ\text{C} + 27.0\,^\circ\text{C}\)
Temperature of the element \(= 1027\,^\circ\text{C}\).

The resistance of a uniform wire is \(R = \dfrac{\rho\,l}{A}\), so the resistivity is \(\rho = \dfrac{R\,A}{l}\). (The current is kept negligibly small so that Joule heating does not change the temperature, and \(\rho\) is that of the material at the temperature of the experiment.)
\(\rho = \dfrac{(5.0\,\Omega)\left(6.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}^2\right)}{15\,\text{m}} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{-6}}{15}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\)
Resistivity \(= 2.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\).

Using \(R_2 = R_1\left[1 + \alpha (T_2 - T_1)\right]\) with the resistance at \(T_1 = 27.5\,^\circ\text{C}\) as the reference,
\(\alpha = \dfrac{R_2 - R_1}{R_1 (T_2 - T_1)}\)
Here \(R_1 = 2.1\,\Omega\), \(R_2 = 2.7\,\Omega\) and \(T_2 - T_1 = 100\,^\circ\text{C} - 27.5\,^\circ\text{C} = 72.5\,^\circ\text{C}\).
\(\alpha = \dfrac{0.6\,\Omega}{(2.1\,\Omega)(72.5\,^\circ\text{C})} = \dfrac{0.6}{152.25}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)
Temperature coefficient of resistivity of silver \(= 3.9 \times 10^{-3}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\) (about \(0.0039\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)).

The initial current is drawn while the element is still at room temperature, so it fixes the resistance at \(T_1 = 27.0\,^\circ\text{C}\); the settled current fixes the resistance at the steady temperature \(T_2\).
\(R_1 = \dfrac{230\,\text{V}}{3.2\,\text{A}} = 71.9\,\Omega\), \(\qquad R_2 = \dfrac{230\,\text{V}}{2.8\,\text{A}} = 82.1\,\Omega\)
Using \(R_2 = R_1\left[1 + \alpha (T_2 - T_1)\right]\) with \(\alpha = 1.70 \times 10^{-4}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\),
\(T_2 - T_1 = \dfrac{R_2 - R_1}{R_1\,\alpha} = \dfrac{82.1 - 71.9}{(71.9)\left(1.70 \times 10^{-4}\right)}\,^\circ\text{C} \approx 840\,^\circ\text{C}\)
\(T_2 = 840\,^\circ\text{C} + 27.0\,^\circ\text{C}\)
Steady temperature of the heating element \(\approx 867\,^\circ\text{C}\).

[Textbook defect in the figure: Fig. 3.20 letters only THREE of its four vertices — A, B and C are labelled and the bottom node is drawn as a bare dot with no letter. The question is still answerable, but the branches cannot all be named from the printed figure. The book's OWN answer key settles the intended label: it reports the currents as \(CD\), \(AD\) and \(BD\), so the unlabelled node is D, and the answer below uses that.] Label the bottom vertex D (the printed figure marks it as a node but leaves it unlettered). The arms are AB \(= 10\,\Omega\), BC \(= 5\,\Omega\), AD \(= 5\,\Omega\), DC \(= 10\,\Omega\) and the bridge arm BD \(= 5\,\Omega\); the \(10\,\text{V}\) cell feeds A and C through a series \(10\,\Omega\) resistor. Since \(\dfrac{10}{5} \neq \dfrac{5}{10}\) the bridge is NOT balanced, so Kirchhoff's rules are needed.
Let \(I_1\) flow A to B, \(I_2\) flow A to D and \(I_g\) flow B to D. The junction rule then gives \(I_1 - I_g\) in BC, \(I_2 + I_g\) in DC and a total \(I = I_1 + I_2\) in the supply branch.
Loop ABDA: \(-10I_1 - 5I_g + 5I_2 = 0\)
Loop BCDB: \(-5(I_1 - I_g) + 10(I_2 + I_g) + 5I_g = 0\)
Loop A-B-C and back through the supply: \(-10I_1 - 5(I_1 - I_g) - 10(I_1 + I_2) + 10 = 0\)
Solving the three equations,
\(I_1 = \dfrac{4}{17}\,\text{A}\), \(\quad I_2 = \dfrac{6}{17}\,\text{A}\), \(\quad I_g = -\dfrac{2}{17}\,\text{A}\)
The negative sign means the bridge current actually flows from D to B. Hence the branch currents are
AB: \(\dfrac{4}{17}\,\text{A} \approx 0.235\,\text{A}\); \(\quad\) BC: \(\dfrac{6}{17}\,\text{A} \approx 0.353\,\text{A}\); \(\quad\) AD: \(\dfrac{6}{17}\,\text{A} \approx 0.353\,\text{A}\); \(\quad\) DC: \(\dfrac{4}{17}\,\text{A} \approx 0.235\,\text{A}\); \(\quad\) BD: \(\dfrac{2}{17}\,\text{A} \approx 0.118\,\text{A}\) from D to B; \(\quad\) supply branch: \(\dfrac{10}{17}\,\text{A} \approx 0.588\,\text{A}\).
As a check, both routes give the same potential difference across the bridge, \(V_{AC} = 10I_1 + 5(I_1 - I_g) = 5I_2 + 10(I_2 + I_g) = \dfrac{70}{17}\,\text{V}\), so the bridge alone is equivalent to \(7\,\Omega\) and the total circuit resistance is \(17\,\Omega\), giving \(I = \dfrac{10\,\text{V}}{17\,\Omega} = \dfrac{10}{17}\,\text{A}\).
Total current drawn from the cell \(= \dfrac{10}{17}\,\text{A} \approx 0.588\,\text{A}\).

During charging the supply drives current backwards through the battery, so the battery's emf opposes the supply and the net driving emf is \(120\,\text{V} - 8.0\,\text{V}\), while the series resistor and the internal resistance are in series.
\(I = \dfrac{120\,\text{V} - 8.0\,\text{V}}{15.5\,\Omega + 0.5\,\Omega} = \dfrac{112\,\text{V}}{16\,\Omega} = 7.0\,\text{A}\)
Because the current is forced INTO the positive terminal, the terminal voltage exceeds the emf by the internal drop:
\(V = \varepsilon + Ir = 8.0\,\text{V} + (7.0\,\text{A})(0.5\,\Omega) = 11.5\,\text{V}\)
(Equivalently, \(V = 120\,\text{V} - (7.0\,\text{A})(15.5\,\Omega) = 11.5\,\text{V}\).)
Purpose of the series resistor: it limits the charging current. Without it the only resistance in the circuit would be the battery's \(0.5\,\Omega\), giving \(I = (120 - 8.0)/0.5 = 224\,\text{A}\) — enough to overheat and destroy the battery. The resistor drops most of the excess supply voltage and keeps the charging current at a safe value.
Terminal voltage during charging \(= 11.5\,\text{V}\).

The drift speed follows from \(I = neAv_d\), with \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\):
\(v_d = \dfrac{I}{neA} = \dfrac{3.0\,\text{A}}{\left(8.5 \times 10^{28}\,\text{m}^{-3}\right)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\right)\left(2.0 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\right)}\)
\(v_d = \dfrac{3.0}{2.72 \times 10^{4}}\,\text{m s}^{-1} = 1.1 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
The time to drift the length \(l = 3.0\,\text{m}\) is
\(t = \dfrac{l}{v_d} = \dfrac{3.0\,\text{m}}{1.1 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}\)
Time taken \(= 2.7 \times 10^{4}\,\text{s}\) (about \(7.6\) hours).
